Kintsvisi Monastery

A 13th-century monastery in the woods, home to the Angel of Kintsvisi — the best-known fresco in Georgian art.

Time needed
2 h
From Tbilisi
125 km · 1:50
Road
Mostly paved
Car needed
Crossover / SUV
Season
May–October
Entry
free

Kintsvisi holds a place in art history because of one fresco, and that fresco genuinely justifies the detour. On the north wall of St Nicholas church an angel announces the Resurrection to the myrrh-bearing women. The face, the softness of the pigment and the lightness of the gesture depart so far from the period standard that the Angel of Kintsvisi has become the emblem of medieval Georgian painting.

The monastery was built around the turn of the 12th and 13th centuries, in the reign of Queen Tamar, at the peak of the Georgian golden age. Three churches stand in the complex, the main one a brick cross-domed church. Inside there are also portraits of Tamar and her son Giorgi Lasha, which makes the building a historical document as well as an artistic one.

The setting matters too. The monastery sits in dense deciduous forest north of Kareli, above a small valley, and in autumn the colour here is remarkable. It is an active monastery with monks in residence, the silence is close to total, and visitor numbers are low.

Kintsvisi is often skipped simply because it lies fifteen kilometres off the motorway — which is precisely why you tend to have it to yourself.

Practical advice

The church door is not always open; if you find it locked, ask at the monastic building. The frescoes are lit only by weak natural light, so come on a sunny day around midday, and flash photography is forbidden. The dress code applies and scarves are left by the door. The last kilometres run through forest and turn muddy after rain. There are no facilities at all — buy water, food and fuel in Kareli. Two hours is ample.

How to get there from Tbilisi

From Tbilisi take the E60 west past Gori to Kareli, about 110 km of fast motorway. Turn north in Kareli and continue 12 to 15 km through villages. Most of that is asphalt, but the final two or three kilometres are narrow, steep and partly gravel through woodland. In total 125 km and roughly an hour and fifty minutes. In dry weather a crossover is comfortable and a sedan is possible with care; after rain you genuinely want ground clearance. Fill up in Gori or Kareli before turning off.
